items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Delia Marsh's 2011 novel The Quiet Needle. Ines, a newly hired technician, is spending her first night at a remote seismic monitoring station.

Ines had always pictured seismology as a dull business of numbers, and she had taken the station job mostly for the salary. Yet when the recording drum began to turn and the needle traced the faint tremors of a quake hundreds of miles away, she found she could not look away. She pulled her chair closer. Each small flicker of ink seemed to her a message from deep inside the earth, and she stayed awake until dawn, waiting for the next one.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how the station's instruments record earthquakes that occur far away
To portray Ines's growing fascination with work she had expected to find dull
To show Ines's regret at having accepted a job only for the salary it paid
To reveal how Ines first became interested in studying earthquakes as a child
items.explanation: The setup line tells you Ines is the focus. The excerpt opens with what she used to believe (seismology is dull), then turns on 'Yet': she can't look away, pulls her chair closer, and stays up until dawn. Taken as a whole, the excerpt shows her becoming fascinated by work she expected to be boring, and that is what B says.

A.why: You picked a choice about the drum and needle, which are incidental details. The excerpt never explains how the instruments work. It uses them to show how Ines reacts. This is the content trap: the choice describes things in the text and ignores what the excerpt is doing.

C.why: You went with the salary detail and missed the turn at 'Yet.' Ines does not regret taking the job. She is so absorbed that she stays awake until dawn, which is the opposite of regret.

D.why: You added a detail the text never gives. The excerpt says nothing about Ines's childhood. In fact, it says she used to think seismology was dull. Stick to what the excerpt as a whole conveys.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Varga's 1998 poem "For the Bridge Builders."

They say the river does not remember who tamed it,
that no plaque will ever carry your names.
But you who sink the pilings in the cold brown current,
who bolt the girders while the wind leans hard,
look up: each morning thousands cross the water
on the strength of what your hands have set.
Build on. The far bank is waiting,
and the span you raise will hold for years.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To warn the bridge builders about the dangers of working above a river in high winds
To describe the materials and methods used to construct a bridge across a river
To criticize the public for failing to learn the names of the people who build bridges
To encourage the bridge builders by affirming the lasting value of their labor
items.explanation: The poem speaks to the builders ('you who sink the pilings'). It first states a discouraging view, that nobody will remember them, and then corrects it with 'But.' After that it points to the thousands who cross the bridge every day and urges the builders to 'Build on' because their span 'will hold for years.' The tone is encouraging, so D is correct.

A.why: You reversed the poem's tone. The wind and cold current show how hard the work is, but the poem never warns the builders. It cheers them on with 'Build on.' Encouraging is not the same as warning.

B.why: You noticed the pilings and girders and took them to be the point. The poem mentions these details only to honor the people doing the work. It never explains how a bridge is built.

C.why: You read too much into the line about no plaque. The poem mentions that the builders go unnamed only so it can answer that worry. It never blames the public. The speaker's attention stays on the builders the whole time.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Hal Bergstrom's 2004 memoir Forty Acres East. A soil scientist has persuaded the narrator's father to let her test a new planting method on one strip of the family's farm.

My father had farmed the same way for thirty years and trusted nothing that came out of a university. When the scientist marked off her strip of clover-covered rows, he stood at the fence with his arms folded and said nothing. But all that summer I caught him walking out to that strip at dusk, crouching to press the dark soil between his fingers, then glancing back at his own dry rows. By August he had stopped pretending not to care.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray the father's quiet, growing interest in a method he had first distrusted
To convey the narrator's own wish to become a soil scientist after that summer
To explain why the clover method produced richer soil than the father's method
To show the father's open hostility toward the scientist throughout the summer
items.explanation: Even though the narrator tells the story, the excerpt is about the father. He starts out distrustful, with folded arms and nothing to say. After 'But,' he keeps going back to the test strip to feel the soil, and by August he has 'stopped pretending not to care.' A names the right person and the right change.

B.why: You shifted the focus from the father to the narrator and added a wish the text never mentions. The narrator only watches. Nothing in the excerpt says the narrator wants a career in soil science.

C.why: You noticed the 'dark soil' next to the 'dry rows' and assumed the excerpt is about the science. It never says why the clover method works. That contrast is there to show the father's reaction.

D.why: You stopped reading after the folded arms. The father is silent at the start, not openly hostile, and over the summer he softens. 'Throughout the summer' contradicts the change the excerpt shows.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Priya Nandakumar's 2015 novel The Piece Rate. Jonah works at a garment factory where pay is about to change from an hourly wage to a set amount for each finished shirt.

The foreman announced the change as though it were a gift: from now on, every shirt would earn its own wage. Jonah, however, did the arithmetic in his head and felt his stomach tighten. He was careful, not fast, and he knew it. Around him, the younger workers were already grinning and flexing their fingers. Jonah bent over his machine and tried to make his hands move quicker, but every crooked seam he had to tear out seemed to cost him more than thread.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray the younger workers' excitement about earning more under the new system
To explain why the factory's owners decided to change how the workers would be paid
To convey Jonah's anxiety that the new pay system will leave him worse off
To show Jonah's relief that his careful work will finally be properly rewarded
items.explanation: The setup line names Jonah as the focus. The foreman presents the change as a gift, and 'however' turns to Jonah's reaction: his stomach tightens, he knows he is slow, and every mistake now 'cost him more than thread.' The excerpt as a whole conveys his worry that pay per shirt will hurt him, so C is correct.

A.why: You chose a character who is in the excerpt but is not its focus. The grinning younger workers get one sentence, and they are there to contrast with Jonah. The excerpt is about his feelings, not theirs.

B.why: You chose a detail the text never gives. The excerpt says nothing about why the owners changed the pay system. It only shows how Jonah reacts to the change.

D.why: You reversed Jonah's feeling. Being careful instead of fast is exactly why he expects to lose under the new system, so he is anxious, not relieved.

The following text is adapted from Clara Wendell's 1919 novel The Gauge-Keeper. Ada has just been hired to record the daily water level of the river near her family's farm.

To portray Ada's growing fascination with the river as she records its levels
To describe how Ada learned to predict floods before they reached the farm

To describe how the city's current street layout was first developed

To convey the narrator's realization that his father's silence meant approval

B.why: You misread the opening. The narrator expected his father to inspect the joints. He never says he feared they were flawed, and the excerpt ends with approval, not worry.

C.why: You picked a background detail. The trucks only set the scene while the father stands on the bridge. The excerpt is not about how bridges are tested.

You will be wrong. The sky will change its mind

To describe the way clouds shift between the evening map and the morning
To recount a time when the speaker's own forecast of rain proved wrong
To encourage a young forecaster to keep going despite inevitable errors

The following text is adapted from Maren Halloway's 2009 novel The Long Exposure. Ruth, an amateur astronomer, has been photographing the night sky using her late father's observing notes.

Ruth had promised herself she would mail the plates to the observatory by Friday. The comet sat on the third plate exactly where her father's notebook said it would return, a smudge no wider than an eyelash. Once professionals confirmed it, the orbit would be printed in the catalog under his name, and the notebook would become a footnote. She slid the plate back into its sleeve, then took it out again, and held it to the window until the light went.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray Ruth's pride that her father's long-ago prediction about the comet has finally proved correct
To convey Ruth's reluctance to give up something private even as she prepares to honor her father publicly
To illustrate the patience her father showed in tracking the comet's orbit across many years of observation
To suggest that Ruth has begun to doubt whether the smudge on the plate is really the returning comet
items.explanation: Your focus is Ruth. Mailing the plates will put her father's name in the catalog, which is a public honor. It will also turn his notebook, her private link to him, into 'a footnote.' She puts the plate away and then takes it out again, so she is putting off a step she has already promised to take. The excerpt as a whole shows her torn between honoring him and keeping something for herself.

A.why: You correctly saw that the father's prediction was confirmed, then assumed Ruth must feel proud. The text never names pride. Her actions after the confirmation show hesitation, and that is what the excerpt is built around.

C.why: You moved the focus from Ruth to her father. His notebook is the background. The excerpt is about what Ruth does with the plate, not about how he worked.

D.why: The comet sits 'exactly where' the notebook predicted, so Ruth has no reason to doubt it. You read her handling of the plate as uncertainty about the image. It is really hesitation about letting it go.

The following text is adapted from Tomás Eberle's 2014 memoir Drawn Lines. Early in his career, Eberle worked as a junior planner on a city's waterfront redesign.

On the drawings the new promenade was a clean gray ribbon, and I had drawn most of it. I was proudest of the gentle curve at the ferry landing; the director called it the best line in the set. Walking the site the week before demolition, I found that the curve passed directly over Mrs. Albescu's bench, where she had fed pigeons every morning for as long as anyone at the bakery could remember. I went back to the office and said nothing.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To show the narrator's pride in a design feature that his director singled out for special praise
To criticize the director for approving a plan that ignored the daily routines of local residents
To recount the narrator's discovery that his best work carries a cost he chooses not to raise
To describe how Mrs. Albescu responded when she learned that her bench was to be removed
items.explanation: Sketch the order: pride in the curve, then the discovery that it erases Mrs. Albescu's bench, then silence. The excerpt is about the narrator. His proudest line costs something the neighborhood treasures, and he decides not to mention it. Only this choice covers both the discovery and the silence.

A.why: You stopped after the first two sentences. The pride is only the setup. The site visit overturns it, and a choice that leaves out the turn misses the purpose of the whole excerpt.

B.why: You moved the blame to the director. The director only praises the curve. The narrator drew it, found the problem, and kept quiet, so the excerpt is about him.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Ada Krell's 1998 poem "For the Night Inspector." The speaker addresses a person who inspects a city bridge.

You walk the girders while the city sleeps,
tapping each rivet like a doctor's knuckle
against a chest, listening for the hollow note.
By morning you are gone. The buses cross,
the joggers cross, a boy with a kite crosses,
and none of them will think of you at all—
which is the whole of what you meant to build:
a day so ordinary no one thanks it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To warn the inspector that a flaw in the bridge could go unnoticed during a night inspection
To compare the inspector's careful work on the bridge to a doctor's examination of a patient
To lament that the inspector's careful labor goes unthanked by the people who depend on it
To honor the inspector by presenting the public's unawareness as proof of the work's success
items.explanation: The turn comes at the dash: people's forgetting the inspector is 'the whole of what you meant to build.' An ordinary day nobody thanks is the goal of the work, not an injustice. The speaker is paying tribute, and the people's unawareness is how the poem measures the inspector's success.

A.why: You treated 'listening for the hollow note' as a warning. Nothing in the poem suggests a flaw gets missed. The bridge carries everyone safely, and the tone is admiring, not anxious.

B.why: The doctor comparison is one simile in the second line. You chose an image the poem uses and treated it as the poem's purpose.

C.why: You correctly saw that no one thinks of the inspector, then read that as sad. The final lines say this unawareness is exactly what the inspector meant to build, so the tone is tribute, not lament.

The following text is adapted from Priya Venkataraman's 2017 novel Dry Season. Lakshmi, an agricultural scientist, is setting up trial plots of a drought-tolerant millet on her grandfather's farm.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray the grandfather's movement from wary skepticism toward a willingness to join her work
To show Lakshmi's determination to modernize the farm in spite of her grandfather's objections
To convey the grandfather's insistence that his way of planting is superior to scientific trials
To explain why the new variety of millet is expected to perform better in a dry growing season

C.why: You read the first half and stopped. The 'But' turns the paragraph, and the grandfather ends up taking part in the trial rather than resisting it.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Henrik Solberg's 2003 short story "Soundings." Ilse works in a coastal survey office, revising a nautical chart.

The new soundings moved the sandbar forty meters east. Ilse erased the old line carefully, as she had been taught, leaving no ghost of it on the vellum. Her predecessor had drawn that line in 1958, and three generations of captains had trusted it. She inked the new curve, checked it twice, and then, in pencil small enough to pass for a flaw in the paper, wrote his initials in the margin beside it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To show Ilse's reluctance to make a correction that will erase the work of her predecessor
To portray Ilse's quiet wish to acknowledge her predecessor while making a needed correction
To convey Ilse's disapproval of her predecessor for an error that misled many captains
To describe the procedures a survey office follows when it updates an existing chart
items.explanation: Ilse does the correction thoroughly. She erases the old line without a trace, inks the new curve, and checks it twice. Then she adds the predecessor's initials so small they could pass for a flaw in the paper. She does the job fully and still finds a private way to credit the man whose line she replaced.

A.why: You saw that Ilse respects her predecessor and assumed she must hesitate to correct him. She doesn't hesitate. She erases 'carefully, as she had been taught' and checks the new line twice. The respect comes after the correction, not instead of it.

C.why: Writing his initials beside the new line is a tribute, not a criticism. The captains 'trusted' the old line, and the text never says it misled them.

D.why: The procedural details are there, but they set up Ilse's private gesture. A choice about office procedure leaves out the character the excerpt is about.

The following text is adapted from June Okafor's 2011 memoir The Reversed Image. Okafor recalls her first year as an apprentice in a woodcut studio.

My teacher pulled a proof from the block I had spent three weeks carving and laid it on the table without a word. The lines were clean; I had checked every one with a loupe. items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To show the teacher's approval of the precise technique his apprentice had worked to master
To depict the narrator's satisfaction with a print whose lines she had inspected so closely
To explain why the teacher judged the birds in the narrator's print to be poorly carved
To convey the narrator's delayed realization that narrow praise hid her teacher's disappointment

B.why: Her confidence after checking with a loupe is only the starting point. The excerpt ends with that confidence undercut, and this choice leaves out the realization.

C.why: The teacher gives no reason and says nothing about the birds at all. You supplied a judgment the text leaves unspoken.

The following text is from Sofía Marend's 2015 poem "Field Recording." The speaker, a linguist, addresses an elderly woman who is the last fluent speaker of her language.

Say it again, the word for the river in spring—
the levels are right now; the red light holds.
The machine will keep your vowel, the small catch
before the final stop, exactly.
It will not keep the way you turned to the window
to find the word, as if the river told you,
or how you laughed when I said it back wrong.
Say it again. I am getting everything but you.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To express the speaker's awareness that the recording can capture the woman's words but not her presence
To celebrate the recording's power to preserve the woman's language exactly as she speaks it
To urge the woman to speak more clearly so that the recording of her language will be accurate
To apologize to the woman for having mispronounced her word for the river in spring
items.explanation: The poem turns on 'will keep' versus 'will not keep.' The machine records the sounds exactly. It misses her turn toward the window and her laugh. The last line says it directly: 'everything but you.' The purpose is the speaker's recognition of what a recording cannot hold.

B.why: You saw that 'exactly' praises the machine and stopped there. The next three lines list what it cannot keep, and the closing line makes that loss the point of the poem.

C.why: 'Say it again' is a recording request, not a complaint about her speech. The speaker says the machine already gets her vowel 'exactly,' so clarity is never the problem.

D.why: The mispronunciation is one remembered moment, and it is offered as something precious, her laugh. You took an incidental detail for the poem's purpose.
